DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Claim Objections
Claim 19 is objected to because of the following informalities: Claim 19 recites the limitations “wherein a duration of each annealing of the gate insulation layer is at least 10 minutes and at most 600 minutes” However there is only a recitation of one annealing performed. It is believed that the word “each” should be removed in order to correct this informality.  Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(a)(1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
Claim(s) 1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 15, and 17-19 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by US 20160126092 (Makifuchi et al).
Concerning claim 1, Makifuchi discloses a method for forming a wide band gap semiconductor device (Fig. 7), the method comprising: forming a gate insulation layer (18) on a wide band gap semiconductor substrate (7) ([0063] and [0068]); and annealing the gate insulation layer using at least a first reactive gas species and at least a second reactive gas species, wherein the first reactive gas species differs from the second reactive gas species ([0068], note that the a POA (post oxidation anneal) is done in an atmosphere including H2 and H2O with H2  being the first reactive gas species and H2O being the second reactive gas species).
Continuing to claim 3, Makifuchi discloses wherein annealing the gate insulation layer is performed in a reactive gas atmosphere comprising at least 0.1 vol% of the first reactive gas species and at least 0.1 vol% of the second reactive gas species at the same time ([0068], note that the concentration of H2O is set to be 73% with the remaining being H2).
Considering claim 4, Makifuchi discloses wherein the first reactive gas species is one of nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, hydrogen, ammonia, hydrogen peroxide, nitric acid, water vapor, phosphoryl chloride, and oxygen ([0068], H2  being the first reactive gas species), and wherein the second reactive gas species is another one of nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, hydrogen, ammonia, hydrogen peroxide, nitric acid, water vapor, phosphoryl chloride, and oxygen ([0068], H2O being the second reactive gas species).
Referring to claim 7, Makifuchi discloses after the annealing of the gate insulation layer using at least the first reactive gas species and at least the second reactive gas species, annealing the gate insulation layer in an inert gas atmosphere ([0068], note that a heating is done after the POA in a nitrogen (inert) atmosphere).
Regarding claim 8, Makifuchi discloses wherein the annealing of the gate insulation layer in the inert gas atmosphere comprises: heating the gate insulation layer in the inert gas atmosphere at a temperature lower than 1200°C to reduce a hydrogen concentration within the gate insulation layer ([0068], note that the heating is done directly after the POA which is completed at 1000 ºC with no recitation of the temperature being increased and therefore the examiner is interpreting that the temperature of the heating is done at 1000 ºC).
Pertaining to claim 11, Makifuchi discloses wherein the inert gas atmosphere has a concentration of oxygen of at most 0.5vol% ([0068], note that a heating is done after the POA in a nitrogen (inert) atmosphere which the examiner interprets to mean 100 vol% which would make the concentration of oxygen 0 vol%).
As to claim 13, Makifuchi discloses wherein an annealing temperature of each annealing of the gate insulation layer is at least 600°C and at most 1200°C ([0068], note that the heating is done directly after the POA which is completed at 1000 ºC with no recitation of the temperature being increased and therefore the examiner is interpreting that the temperature of the heating is done at 1000 ºC).
Concerning claim 15, Makifuchi discloses further comprising: after the annealing of the gate insulation layer using at least the first reactive gas species and at least the second reactive gas species, forming a gate electrode (19) on the gate insulation layer (Fig. 7 and [0071]).
Continuing to claim 17, Makifuchi discloses wherein the wide band gap semiconductor substrate is a silicon carbide substrate ([0063]).
Considering claim 18, Makifuchi discloses wherein the gate insulation layer is a silicon dioxide layer ([0068]).
Referring to claim 19, Makifuchi discloses a method for forming a wide band gap semiconductor device (Fig. 7), the method comprising: forming a gate insulation layer (18) on a wide band gap semiconductor substrate (7) ([0063] and [0068]); and annealing the gate insulation layer using at least a first reactive gas species and at least a second reactive gas species, wherein the first reactive gas species differs from the second reactive gas species ([0068], note that the a POA (post oxidation anneal) is done in an atmosphere including H2 and H2O with H2  being the first reactive gas species and H2O being the second reactive gas species), wherein annealing the gate insulation layer is performed in a reactive gas atmosphere comprising at least 0.1 vol% of the first reactive gas species and at least 0.1 vol% of the second reactive gas species at the same time ([0068], note that the concentration of H2O is set to be 73% with the remaining being H2), wherein a duration of each annealing of the gate insulation layer is at least 10 minutes and at most 600 minutes ([0068], note that the POA (post oxidation anneal) is performed for 30 minutes).
Claim(s) 1,  3, and 18 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by US 9945030 (DesOrmeaux et al).
Regarding claim 1, DesOrmeaux discloses a method for forming a wide band gap semiconductor device (Fig. 10), the method comprising: forming a gate insulation layer (col. 5 lines 1-5) on a wide band gap semiconductor substrate (col. 4 lines 35-41, note that a GaN substrate is disclosed as one of the substrate materials which the examiner is relying on being the wide and gap semiconductor substrate); and annealing the gate insulation layer using at least a first reactive gas species and at least a second reactive gas species, wherein the first reactive gas species differs from the second reactive gas species (col. 5 lines 10-23, note that the atmosphere for the annealing is disclosed to be comprise 1% to 10% by volume hydrogen gas and 90% to 99% by volume nitrogen gas, inert gas, or a mixture of both, and the atmosphere comprising 0.001% to 100% by volume hydrogen with hydrogen being the second reactive gas species and nitrogen being the first reactive gas species).
Pertaining to claim 3, DesOrmeaux discloses wherein annealing the gate insulation layer is performed in a reactive gas atmosphere comprising at least 0.1 vol% of the first reactive gas species and at least 0.1 vol% of the second reactive gas species at the same time (col. 5 lines 10-23, note that the atmosphere for the annealing is disclosed to be comprise 1% to 10% by volume hydrogen gas and 90% to 99% by volume nitrogen gas, inert gas, or a mixture of both, with hydrogen being the second reactive gas species and nitrogen being the first reactive gas species).
As to claim 18,  DesOrmeaux discloses wherein the gate insulation layer is a silicon dioxide layer (col. 5 lines 1-5).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claim(s) 2, 7, and  8 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over US 9945030 (DesOrmeaux et al) as applied to claim 1 above, and further in view of US 20160126092 (Makifuchi et al).
As to claim 2, DesOrmeaux discloses wherein annealing the gate insulation layer comprises at least a first annealing process (col. 5 lines 10-23, note that the atmosphere for the annealing is disclosed to be comprise 1% to 10% by volume hydrogen gas and 90% to 99% by volume nitrogen gas, inert gas, or a mixture of both, with hydrogen being the second reactive gas species and nitrogen being the first reactive gas species),  . . . . wherein the first annealing process is performed in a reactive gas atmosphere comprising at least 0.1 vol% of the first reactive gas species and at most 0.1 vol% of the second reactive gas species (col. 5 lines 10-23, note that the atmosphere for the annealing is disclosed to be comprise 1% to 10% by volume hydrogen gas and 90% to 99% by volume nitrogen gas, inert gas, or a mixture of both, with hydrogen being the second reactive gas species and nitrogen being the first reactive gas species).
DesOrmeaux does not disclose  at least a second annealing process wherein the second annealing process is performed after the first annealing process and wherein the second annealing process is performed in a reactive gas atmosphere comprising at least 0.l vol% of the second reactive gas species and at most 0.1vol% of the first reactive gas species. However Makifuchi discloses a method for forming a wide band gap semiconductor device (Fig. 7), the method comprising: forming a gate insulation layer (18) on a wide band gap semiconductor substrate (7) ([0063] and [0068]); and annealing the gate insulation layer using at least a first reactive gas species and at least a second reactive gas species, wherein the first reactive gas species differs from the second reactive gas species, at least a second annealing process wherein the second annealing process is performed after the first annealing process and wherein the second annealing process is performed in a reactive gas atmosphere comprising at least 0.l vol% of the second reactive gas species and at most 0.1vol% of the first reactive gas species ([0068], the heating is performed in a Hydrogen atmosphere in which no other gases are disclosed as being supplied so the vol% of the reactive gas atmosphere is 100% Hydrogen and therefore has at least 0.1 vol% of the first reactive gas and at most 0.1 vol% of the second reactive gas with the vol % of the second gas being 0%). Makifuchi also discloses that this process can reduce interface state density in silicon carbide semiconductor devices ([0003]). Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the invention to perform a second annealing after the first anneal such that the second annealing process is performed in a reactive gas atmosphere comprising at least 0.l vol% of the second reactive gas species and at most 0.1vol% of the first reactive gas species as disclosed by Makifuchi in order to reduce interface state density in silicon carbide semiconductor devices.
Concerning claim 7, DesOrmeaux discloses  . . . . annealing of the gate insulation layer using at least the first reactive gas species and at least the second reactive gas species (col. 5 lines 10-23).
DesOrmeaux does not disclose after the annealing of the gate insulation layer using at least the first reactive gas species and at least the second reactive gas species,  annealing the gate insulation layer in an inert gas atmosphere.
However, Makifuchi discloses a method for forming a wide band gap semiconductor device (Fig. 7), the method comprising: forming a gate insulation layer (18) on a wide band gap semiconductor substrate (7) ([0063] and [0068]); and annealing the gate insulation layer using at least a first reactive gas species and at least a second reactive gas species, wherein the first reactive gas species differs from the second reactive gas species, and after the annealing of the gate insulation layer using at least the first reactive gas species and at least the second reactive gas species,  annealing the gate insulation layer in an inert gas atmosphere. ([0068], note that a heating is done after the POA in a nitrogen (inert) atmosphere). Makifuchi also discloses that this process can reduce interface state density in silicon carbide semiconductor devices ([0003]). Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the invention to perform a second annealing after the first anneal such that the second annealing process is performed in a reactive gas atmosphere comprising at least 0.l vol% of the second reactive gas species and at most 0.1vol% of the first reactive gas species as disclosed by Makifuchi in order to reduce interface state density in silicon carbide semiconductor devices.
Continuing to claim 8, DesOrmeaux in view of Makifuchi discloses wherein the annealing of the gate insulation layer in the inert gas atmosphere comprises: heating the gate insulation layer in the inert gas atmosphere at a temperature lower than 1200°C to reduce a hydrogen concentration within the gate insulation layer (Makifuchi [0068], note that the heating is done directly after the POA which is completed at 1000 ºC with no recitation of the temperature being increased and therefore the examiner is interpreting that the temperature of the heating is done at 1000 ºC).
Claim(s) 5, 6, and 9 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over US 9945030 (DesOrmeaux et al) in view of US 20160126092 (Makifuchi et al) as applied to claim 1 above, and further in view of US 20140302687 (Ashihara et al).
Considering claim 5, DesOrmeaux in view of Makifuchi discloses wherein the first reactive gas species is diluted with an inert gas during the annealing of the gate insulation layer so that a volume percent of the first reactive gas species is at least 1vol% and at most 50vol% (DesOrmeaux col. 5 lines 10-23, note that the atmosphere for the annealing is disclosed to be comprise 1% to 10% by volume hydrogen gas and 90% to 99% by volume nitrogen gas, inert gas, or a mixture of both, with hydrogen being the second reactive gas species and nitrogen being the first reactive gas species),
DesOrmeaux in view of Makifuchi does not disclose wherein the first reactive gas species is nitric oxide. However, Ashihara discloses performing an annealing treatment on a silicon oxide insulating film in order to improve the quality of the film and using nitric oxide and ammonia as reaction gases for that annealing treatment ([0066]). Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the invention to use nitric oxide as the first reactive species because it is known in the art to be a good reactive species for use in an annealing treatment on silicon oxide insulating layers to improve the quality of the film.
Referring to claim 6, DesOrmeaux in view of Makifuchi discloses wherein the second reactive gas species is diluted with an inert gas during the annealing of the gate insulation layer so that a volume percent of the second reactive gas species is at least 0.1vol% and at most 10vol% (col. 5 lines 10-23, note that the atmosphere for the annealing is disclosed to be comprise 1% to 10% by volume hydrogen gas and 90% to 99% by volume nitrogen gas, inert gas, or a mixture of both, with hydrogen being the second reactive gas species and nitrogen being the first reactive gas species)
DesOrmeaux in view of Makifuchi does not disclose wherein the second reactive gas species is ammonia. However, Ashihara discloses performing an annealing treatment on a silicon oxide insulating film in order to improve the quality of the film and using nitric oxide and ammonia as reaction gases for that annealing treatment ([0066]). Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the invention to use ammonia as the second reactive species because it is known in the art to be a good reactive species for use in an annealing treatment on silicon oxide insulating layers to improve the quality of the film.
Regarding claim 9, DesOrmeaux in view of Makifuchi discloses. . . . wherein a volume percent of the first reactive gas species and/or the second reactive gas species is at least 0.1vol% (col. 5 lines 10-23, note that the atmosphere for the annealing is disclosed to be comprise 1% to 10% by volume hydrogen gas and 90% to 99% by volume nitrogen gas, inert gas, or a mixture of both, with hydrogen being the second reactive gas species and nitrogen being the first reactive gas species).
DesOrmeaux in view of Makifuchi does not disclose  wherein the first reactive gas species and/or the second reactive gas species comprises at least one of nitric oxide and ammonia. However, Ashihara discloses performing an annealing treatment on a silicon oxide insulating film in order to improve the quality of the film and using nitric oxide and ammonia as reaction gases for that annealing treatment ([0066]). Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the invention to use nitric oxide  or ammonia as the first reactive or second reactive species because they are known in the art to be good reactive species for use in an annealing treatment on silicon oxide insulating layers to improve the quality of the film.
Claim(s) 10 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over US 9945030 (DesOrmeaux et al) in view of US 20160126092 (Makifuchi et al) as applied to claim 8 above, and further in view of US 20080026553 (Chua et al).
Pertaining to claim 10, DesOrmeaux in view of Makifuchi discloses wherein the inert gas species comprises at least 90% nitrogen (Makifuchi [0068], note that a heating is done after the POA in a nitrogen (inert) atmosphere).
DesOrmeaux in view of Makifuchi does not disclose  wherein the first reactive gas species and/or the second reactive gas species comprises at least 5 vol% nitric oxide and wherein a duration of the annealing in the inert gas species is shorter than a duration of the annealing in the first reactive gas species and/or the second reactive gas species. However, Chua discloses performing an annealing treatment on a silicon oxide insulating film and using nitric oxide and ammonia as reaction gases for that annealing treatment ([0047]). The selection of a known material based on its suitability for its intended use supported a prima facie obviousness determination in Sinclair & Carroll Co. v. Interchemical Corp., 325 U.S. 327, 65 USPQ 297 (1945). See MPEP 2144.07.  Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the invention to use nitric oxide or ammonia as the first or second reactive species gas because they are known in the art to be good reactive species for use in an annealing treatment on silicon oxide insulating layers.
Additionally, Chua discloses an annealing treatment performed on the silicon oxide insulating layer in an inert atmosphere (note that the chamber is purged with Nitrogen and then an annealing treatment follows the purge and therefore the annealing is done in the purged nitrogen atmosphere) for a duration of 1 second to about 180 seconds ([0044] and [0046]). Chua discloses that process will increase quality and uniformity of the insulating layer ([0007]). Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the invention to perform the annealing in an inert comprising nitrogen for the duration as disclosed by Chua in order to improve quality and uniformity of the insulating layer.
Claim(s) 14 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over US 20160126092 (Makifuchi et al) as applied to claim 1 above, and further in view of US 20080026553 (Chua et al).
As to claim 14, Makifuchi discloses . . . .annealing of the gate insulation layer using at least the first reactive gas species and at least the second reactive gas species ([0068]).
Makifuchi does not disclose before the annealing of the gate insulation layer using at least the first reactive gas species and at least the second reactive gas species heating the gate insulation layer in an inert gas atmosphere at a temperature of at least 950°C.
However, Chua discloses an annealing treatment performed on the silicon oxide insulating layer before a reactive annealing of the silicon oxide layer in an inert atmosphere (note that the chamber is purged with Nitrogen and then an annealing treatment follows the purge and therefore the annealing is done in the purged nitrogen atmosphere) at a temperature between 800 and 1200 degrees Celsius ([0044] and [0046]). Chua discloses that process will increase quality and uniformity of the insulating layer ([0007]). Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the invention to perform the annealing in an inert comprising nitrogen for the duration as disclosed by Chua in order to improve quality and uniformity of the insulating layer.
Claim(s) 14 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable US 9945030 (DesOrmeaux et al) as applied to claim 1 above, and further in view of US 20080026553 (Chua et al).
As to claim 14, DesOrmeaux discloses . . . .annealing of the gate insulation layer using at least the first reactive gas species and at least the second reactive gas species (col. 5 lines 10-23).
DesOrmeaux does not disclose before the annealing of the gate insulation layer using at least the first reactive gas species and at least the second reactive gas species heating the gate insulation layer in an inert gas atmosphere at a temperature of at least 950°C.
However, Chua discloses an annealing treatment performed on the silicon oxide insulating layer before a reactive annealing of the silicon oxide layer in an inert atmosphere (note that the chamber is purged with Nitrogen and then an annealing treatment follows the purge and therefore the annealing is done in the purged nitrogen atmosphere) at a temperature between 800 and 1200 degrees Celsius ([0044] and [0046]). Chua discloses that process will increase quality and uniformity of the insulating layer ([0007]). Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the invention to perform the annealing in an inert comprising nitrogen for the duration as disclosed by Chua in order to improve quality and uniformity of the insulating layer.
Claim(s) 16 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over US 20160126092 (Makifuchi et al) in view of US 20150214047 (Hama et al).
Considering claim 16, Makifuchi discloses forming a gate electrode on a silicon carbide substrate with a treated gate insulating film formed over the substrate.
Makifuchi does not disclose wherein the gate electrode is a gate trench electrode that extends from a surface of the wide band gap semiconductor substrate into the wide band gap semiconductor substrate. Hama discloses forming a gate insulating film on a silicon carbide substrate and performing an annealing process. A trench gate electrode is formed in the substrate. (Fig. 23). In re Dailey, 357 F.2d 669, 149 USPQ 47 (CCPA 1966) (The court held that the configuration of the claimed disposable plastic nursing container was a matter of choice which a person of ordinary skill in the art would have found obvious absent persuasive evidence that the particular configuration of the claimed container was significant.). See MPEP 2144.04 IV B. Therefore absent evidence that configuration of the gate is significant it would have been an obvious change in shape based on device design as disclosed by Hama.
Conclusion
The prior art made of record and not relied upon is considered pertinent to applicant's disclosure. US 20150259796 discloses treatments to a gate insulating layer ([0032]).
